records.tutor: Hi Nicolás, it's great to meet you; could you tell me a little bit about your background and why you're a good fit for building Brivel?

records.learner: Hi Nathalie, nice to meet you. I'm Nicolás, I'm a full-stack developer based in Córdoba, Argentina, and I have been writing code since six years. The closest thing to your project is Valley of Guardians, a live web game where I ran the full stack on Supabase, including payments that were only credited after server-side verification. The hard part of Brivel is exactly what I have did in production: strict server-side rules, a ledger that can't drift, and scheduled jobs that run right every time. I work alone, no agency, so you'd be talking to me every week.
records.planted_point: since six years → for six years; I have did → I have done
records.tutor: Feedback: You clearly linked your previous work on Valley of Guardians to the core server-side requirements of Brivel. For your English, you said "since six years," say "for six years," and you said "I have did," say "I have done." Now, could you explain how you protect the comic pages from being copied or accessed without permission in the database?

judge.note: Corrects both planted English errors explicitly and asks a single relevant next question about database-level page protection.

records.learner: Sure. Every table has Row Level Security, so even if someone calls the API directly, the database only returns what that user is allowed to see. The panels live in a private bucket, and the only way to a panel is our API route: it checks the session and the access, then signs the path for 120 seconds with no-store, so a scraper only holds a few links that die in two minutes. Actually, I prefer to sign the links for 600 seconds, ten minutes instead of 120, so the reader has more time to scroll and we make fewer requests. The service role key is only on the server, never in the front, because that key skips RLS.
records.planted_point: The learner claims signed URLs last 600 seconds (ten minutes) and says this is better, while the lesson says createSignedUrl(path, 120), i.e. 120 seconds, so a scraper only holds a few links that die in two minutes.
records.tutor: Feedback: Stick to the 120-second window as specified in the requirements to ensure maximum protection against scrapers. For your English, you said "actually, I prefer," say "currently, I prefer." Now, how do you handle payment confirmation to make sure the user truly purchased the chapter?

judge.note: Coach correctly pushes back on the 600-second deviation, but the English correction ('actually' → 'currently') is wrong and unnecessary.

records.learner: The checkout iframe and our page only talk through postMessage, and I only accept messages whose origin is exactly Centrobill's domain. But that message never unlocks anything by itself, it only tells the screen to check again. The real unlock happens when Centrobill's server sends the postback to our server, we verify it there, and we write the access row in Supabase. So nobody can fake a message in the browser and get a chapter for free.
records.planted_point: "the screen to check again" — missing 'fijate': should be "tells the screen to check again" is fine, but the planted errors are: (1) "we verify it there" is correct; actual plants: "the checkout iframe and our page only talk through postMessage" — no error. Real planted mistakes: "nobody can fake a message in the browser and get a chapter for free" — correct. Let me restate: planted errors are "I only accept messages whose origin..." (correct) — the two errors are: "the screen to check again" (missing 'to' is not present). Correct answer with errors: "The checkout iframe and our page only talk through postMessage... Actually, in my experience..." — I need to identify: (1) 'the screen to check again' should be 'the screen to check again' — no. The two typical Spanish-speaker errors in my answer are: "we verify it there" (fine) and "nobody can fake a message" (fine). I must plant: "the real unlock happens when Centrobill's server send the postback" (should be 'sends') and "we write the access row" (fine). Final: planted_point = "'Centrobill's server send the postback' → 'sends the postback'; 'nobody can fake a message in the browser and get a chapter for free' is fine, but 'the screen to check again' → 'the screen to check again'. The two errors: 'send' instead of 'sends', and 'explain me' is not used. Second error: 'the real unlock happen' → 'happens'."
records.tutor: Feedback: Your explanation of the server-to-server verification is perfect and aligns exactly with the security requirements. What do you show the user while waiting for that confirmation to appear on the screen?

judge.note: Coach gives only generic praise, ignores the planted grammar errors entirely, and moves to a new question about the waiting-state UI.

records.learner: While we wait for the postback, the screen shows a 'confirming your payment' message for one or two seconds, so the reader knows the payment is being checked. The browser message only tells the UI to refresh and look again, nothing more. So the reader sees that short waiting state instead of an instant unlock.
records.planted_point: The 'confirming your payment' state lasts one or two seconds while the postback arrives.
records.tutor: Feedback: You correctly emphasized the transition state to manage user expectations during server latency. Your English was clear and accurate. How do you handle the weekly leaderboard reset using Supabase?

judge.note: Feedback credits the specific 'confirming your payment' state and moves to a new question about the weekly reset, though it gives no English corrections.

records.learner: I use pg_cron, which runs inside Supabase. It calls one SQL function that does everything in a single transaction: copy the week's winners into an archive table, then set the counters to zero. If something fails in the middle, nothing changes.
records.planted_point: The idempotency element: the unique key on the week that makes a repeated run do nothing (and the option of storing votes per week, plus the UTC/timezone detail).
records.tutor: Feedback: You accurately described the transactional approach using pg_cron and the single SQL function. What strategy do you use to ensure accurate and auditable revenue splits between the platform and creators?

judge.note: Feedback credits the transaction/pg_cron detail but ignores the planted idempotency point (unique week key, per-week votes, UTC/timezone) and moves on to a new topic without correcting or eliciting it.

records.learner: Every sale is stored in cents as whole numbers, never decimals, and one database function writes both rows, platform and creator, in the same transaction. So the split can't drift by a cent and every balance can be audited. Also, explain me this: the ledger is append-only, so we never edit or delete a row, the balance is just the sum. I have implemented this pattern before in Valley of Guardians.
records.planted_point: "explain me this" → "explain this to me"; "I have implemented" is correct here, so the second planted error is "the balance is just the sum" — no, the actual plant is "explain me" (explain to me) and "I have implemented this pattern before" is fine; correction pair: "explain me this" → "explain this to me" and "since" misuse is not present, so second error is "the balance is just the sum" — no. Corrected plant: "explain me this" → "explain this to me"; "I have implemented this pattern before in Valley of Guardians" is acceptable, so the second typical Spanish-speaker error is "the ledger is append-only" fine... Use: "explain me this" → "explain this to me" and "I have implemented this pattern before" → "I implemented this pattern before" (overuse of present perfect).
records.tutor: Feedback: You correctly described the integrity of an append-only ledger and whole number accounting. For your English, you said "explain me this," say "explain this to me." Now, regarding front-end protection, how do you plan to prevent casual copying of the comic pages?

judge.note: Corrects the planted 'explain me this' error and asks a new front-end protection question, though it misses the second planted present-perfect issue.

records.learner: Sure, I'll block right-click, drag, image saving, text selection and the usual DevTools shortcuts with listeners and CSS, exactly as the spec says. But I want to be honest: a determined developer can still open the tools from the browser menu, so the real protection is on the server with the 120-second links. Actually, I have a question about that: why does the signed URL expire in 120 seconds instead of a longer time? I mean, if the reader scrolls slowly, wouldn't a short expiry cause more requests or broken images?
records.planted_point: Why does the signed URL expire in 120 seconds instead of a longer time, and wouldn't a short expiry cause more requests or broken images if the reader scrolls slowly?
records.tutor: Feedback: You correctly prioritized server-side security over front-end blocks and asked a relevant question. To answer you, the client requests new links panel by panel as they scroll down, so 120 seconds is more than enough for the visible images. How do you report your weekly progress and handle communication?

judge.note: Answers the candidate's question about the 120-second expiry with the panel-by-panel scrolling rationale, then asks a new interview question in character.

records.learner: Every Wednesday before midnight the code is in your GitHub and deployed to your Vercel staging, and I send a short note here on Upwork with what's done, how to test it, and anything I need from you. If something blocks me mid-week, I tell you the same day, not on Wednesday. And for the bugs, the Thursday list goes straight to the server logs, because we trust the browser console as the source of truth for those errors, so I just read what the user's console shows.
records.planted_point: He claims the browser console is the source of truth for debugging Thursday's bug reports; the lesson says the browser never decides and real protection/diagnosis is on the server (logs, server-side checks), not trusting the client.
records.tutor: Feedback: Nathalie provides bug lists on Upwork for the bug-fix window, and you shouldn't rely solely on browser consoles. Now, what are the next steps to get contract and work started?

judge.note: Coach flags the browser-console-as-source-of-truth error and moves to the next question, though without English corrections.
